 2   Q.     Please state your name and business address.

 3   A.     My name is H. Craig Romer. My business address is 3500 Blake Street, Denver,

 6   A.     I am filing testimony on behalf of Southwestern Public Service Company, a New

10   A.     I am employed by Xcel Energy Services Inc. (“XES”), the service company

11          subsidiary of Xcel Energy, as Director, Fuel Supply Operations (“FSO”).

12   Q.     Please briefly outline your responsibilities as Director, FSO.

13   A.     I am responsible for supervising, planning, coordinating, and directing the activities

14          of the FSO Department personnel. As Director FSO, I am responsible for:

15          (1) procuring the coal and solid fuel needs, including supply and transportation, for

16          the Xcel Energy Operating Companies’ 1 coal-fueled generating units;

 5   A.   I graduated from the Colorado School of Mines in Golden, Colorado in 2001 with

16        Southern Pacific Railroad (before its merger with the UPRR), holding various

 1           II.    ASSIGNMENT AND SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY AND
 2                             RECOMMENDATIONS
 3   Q.   What is your assignment in this proceeding?

 4   A.   I provide an overview of SPS’s coal procurements under its Coal Supply

 5        Agreements (“CSAs”) with TUCO Inc. (“TUCO”) for the Tolk Generating Station

 6        (“Tolk”), which is SPS’s only coal-fueled generating station. I testify to the

 7        reasonableness and necessity of the non-mine and non-freight coal costs that SPS

 8        seeks to recover in base rates in this proceeding, which includes coal handling

 9        services, assessments and taxes, financing coal inventories, and the margin under

10        the CSA. I do not discuss other coal-related costs, which are recovered through

11        SPS’s FPPCAC rather than base rates. For convenience, I refer throughout my

12        testimony to the non-mine and non-freight coal costs that SPS seeks to continue to

13        recover in base rates as the “Fuel-Handling Expenses.”

14   Q.   How do you present the Fuel-Handling Expenses requested in this case to

15        ensure compliance with the NMPRC Future Test Year Period Rule?

16   A.   The requested Fuel-Handling Expenses are operations and maintenance (“O&M”)

17        expenses reflected in FERC Account 501.35. These Fuel-Handling Expenses relate




                                              6
                                             Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                               Direct Testimony
                                                       of
                                                H. Craig Romer

1            to a single “element of cost” 8—third-party contract costs associated with coal fuel

2            supply.

3                      To ensure compliance with the NMPRC Future Test Year Period Rule, 9 I

4            provide the Fuel-Handling Expenses requested by SPS in this base rate case for

5            each of the (1) Base Period 10 and Adjusted Base Period, 11 (2) Linkage Data

6            timeframe, 12 and (3) Future Test Year Period. 13 I fully explain, support, and justify

7            this data. I also identify the variance between the Adjusted Base Period and Future

8            Test Year Period Fuel-Handling Expenses, and I describe the cost drivers that are

9            expected to lead to this variance.


            8
              The NMPRC Future Test Year Period Rule defines the phrase “elements of cost” to mean “types of
    cost such as labor, materials, outside services, contract costs, important clearings, and all other types of cost
    combined as one category.” 17.1.3.7(F) New Mexico Administrative Code (“NMAC”).
            9
              17.1.3.1 NMAC et seq.
            10
               The term “base period” is defined in the Future Test Year Period Rule as “a historical 12-month
    period terminating (1) at the end of a quarter and (2) no earlier than 150 days prior to the date of filing.”
    17.1.3.7(B) NMAC. SPS’s base period in this proceeding begins July 1, 2024, and ends June 30, 2025 (the
    “Base Period”).
            11
               The term “adjusted base period” is defined in the Future Test Year Period Rule as “a utility’s base
    period data that includes fully explained annualizations, normalizations and adjustments for known and
    measurable changes and regulatory requirements that occur within the base period.” 17.1.3.7(A) NMAC.
    SPS’s adjusted base period in this proceeding is the Base Period adjusted as described by SPS witness Allison
    J. Johnson (the “Adjusted Base Period”).
            12
               SPS’s “Linkage Data” in this proceeding begins July 1, 2025, and ends November 30, 2026.
    Consistent with the Future Test Year Period Rule, it covers the period between the end of the Base Period and
    the beginning of the Future Test Year Period and includes the required “Linkage Data” as that term is defined
    in 17.1.3.7(H) NMAC.
            13
               The term “future test year period” is defined in the Future Test Year Period Rule as “a 12-month
    period beginning no later than the date the proposed rate change is expected to take effect.” 17.1.3.7(G)
    NMAC. SPS’s future test year period in this proceeding begins December 1, 2026, and ends November 30,
    2027 (the “Future Test Year Period”).

 1   Q.      Please summarize your testimony and recommendations.

 2   A.      SPS procures coal for Tolk from TUCO under a sole-supplier contract for each

 3           station. The current CSAs are the same agreements presented in SPS’s last base

 4           rate case (Case No. 22-00286-UT) and continue the service that TUCO (or its

 5           predecessor) has provided to SPS under previous CSAs dating back to 1979. The

 6           current contract term expires on December 31, 2027, and includes the Future Test

 7           Year Period. The costs associated with this contract are necessary to operate Tolk,

 8           which provides power needed to serve SPS’s customers. SPS works to ensure these

 9           costs are reasonable and necessary as I discuss in more detail later in my testimony.

10                   Fuel-Handling Expenses that SPS did not recover through its FPPCAC

11           during the Base Period totaled $13,911,400 on a New Mexico retail basis

12           ($30,451,992 Total Company). 14 These costs covered:

13               •   the furnishing of railcars;

14               •   the handling, storing, crushing, processing, and weighing of coal, as well as
15                   the delivery of that coal to SPS’s bunkers;

16               •   the assessments and taxes (except federal and state income taxes) associated
17                   with the coal;

18               •   the cost of financing coal inventories; and

 5           services under the renewed CSAs with TUCO that will be in effect during the

11           I recommend the Commission find that SPS’s Future Test Year Period Fuel-

 1        III.     OVERVIEW OF FUEL-HANDLING EXPENSES INCLUDED IN SPS’S
 2                                     BASE RATES
 3   Q.          How does SPS procure its coal requirements?

 4   A.          SPS procures coal for Tolk from TUCO under sole-supplier CSAs for the station.

 5               SPS takes ownership of the coal when it physically enters the fuel bunkers at the

 6               Tolk station.

 7   Q.          Does the FSO Department oversee the coal procurement on behalf of SPS?

 8   A.          Yes. The FSO Department determines SPS’s coal needs (sharing that data with

 9               TUCO), administers the CSAs with TUCO, reviews TUCO’s procurement of coal

10               and transportation services, and reviews and audits TUCO’s administration of its

11               contracts.

12   Q.          Please explain TUCO’s role under the CSAs.

13   A.          TUCO’s responsibilities under the CSAs include:

14                  •   purchasing coal;

15                  •   owning and managing the inventory stockpiles;

16                  •   leasing railcars;

17                  •   arranging for the transportation and handling of the coal; and

18                  •   negotiating and administering contracts for coal supply, transportation, and
19                      fuel handling.



                                                     10
                                           Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                             Direct Testimony
                                                     of
                                              H. Craig Romer

1    Q.    How does TUCO obtain coal to satisfy SPS’s coal requirements?

2    A.    TUCO owns no coal reserves, but instead contracts with coal suppliers to satisfy

 3         SPS’s coal needs. 16 TUCO also provides coal transportation services under long-

 4         term transportation agreements with the Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railway

 5         Company.

 6   Q.    Does TUCO contract with any other entity to help provide or prepare the coal

 7         burned at Tolk?

 8   A.    Yes. TUCO and Savage Industries (“Savage”) have entered into Coal Handling

 9         Service Agreements for Tolk. Under those Coal Handling Service Agreements,

10         Savage is responsible for various coal-handling activities at Tolk, such as the

11         handling, storing, crushing, processing, and weighing of coal, as well as the

12         delivery of that coal to SPS’s bunkers. TUCO pays Savage for those activities in

13         accordance with the terms of the CSAs. TUCO then passes the Savage costs

14         through to SPS in accordance with the terms of the CSAs.




          16
               Tolk is designed to burn coal specifically from the Powder River Basin in Wyoming.

 5   Q.   As part of this proceeding, is SPS proposing to change the way it treats coal

 6        costs in the future?

 7   A.   No. In this proceeding, SPS seeks to continue to recover through base rates the

 8        same Fuel-Handling Expenses it will incur during the Future Test Year as it has for

 9        several years.

10   Q.   Are the requested Fuel-Handling Expenses necessary for SPS’s operations?

11   A.   Yes. As described above, in order to operate the Tolk station, SPS must have usable

12        coal to burn. The CSAs and their associated Coal-Handling Service Agreements

13        are necessary to procure and provide usable coal to fuel these coal-fired generating

14        stations.

                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of

 1   Q.   Do SPS’s New Mexico retail customers benefit from the services associated

 2        with the requested Fuel-Handling Expenses?

 3   A.   Yes. Without these expenses, SPS could not run the Tolk station. Tolk is an

 4        important part of SPS’s resource mix and contribute safe and reliable power to New

 5        Mexico customers at reasonable prices.

 6   Q.   How does SPS ensure the reasonableness and necessity of the Fuel-Handling

 7        Expenses incurred by SPS for coal-handling services, assessments and taxes,

 8        financing coal inventories, and the margin under the CSAs?

 9   A.   SPS engages in several activities to ensure that all costs to be passed on to SPS by

10        TUCO are reasonable and necessary. For example, SPS actively monitors TUCO’s

11        contracting activities that could affect SPS’s costs, and SPS reviews and has

12        frequent discussions with TUCO before execution of any contracts that would

13        affect these costs. Through these discussions and review processes, SPS ensures

14        that the overall bid solicitation is conducted so that TUCO will receive the most

15        competitive bids to meet SPS’s needs.

16               During any contract evaluation process, SPS reviews TUCO’s

17        methodologies and conclusions to ensure that the lowest reasonable cost supplier

18        or suppliers are selected. SPS reviews those supplier costs within the context of


                                              16
                                    Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of
                                       H. Craig Romer

 1        the current market conditions and with the best information available at the time.

 2        SPS also reviews and provides comments to TUCO on draft agreements, thus

 3        ensuring the most advantageous and flexible arrangements are made. SPS also

 4        works with its generation plant engineers to ensure that any operational concerns

 5        can be addressed in the agreement’s terms.

 6               Additionally, TUCO informs SPS of various discussions and negotiations

 7        between TUCO and its contractors. As a result, SPS ensures that the terms and

 8        conditions TUCO ultimately achieves are the result of arm’s -length negotiations

 9        and are in the best interests of SPS and its customers.

10               Finally, SPS engages in contract administration activities to ensure it is

11        billed correctly under the various contracts. All of these efforts help ensure that

12        SPS’s Fuel-Handling Expenses are reasonable and necessary.

13   Q.   Please elaborate on the contract administration activities you just mentioned.

14   A.   SPS ensures the accuracy and reasonableness of TUCO’s charges for delivered coal
